central_question: Why does your voice sound different when you hear a recording?
hook: You hear your own voice through a secret tunnel that the microphone can’t see. When you listen to a recording, that tunnel disappears and the sound feels foreign.
aha_moment: The brain normally hears your voice via both air‑conduction and bone‑conduction; a recording captures only the airborne part, leaving out the low‑frequency bone‑conduction boost and tactile feedback that make your voice feel deep and familiar.

story_arc.reveal: Your recorded voice feels higher and lighter than the voice you hear while speaking.

story_arc.purpose: Opening Promise – hint at the hidden mechanism
story_arc.reveal: We’ll uncover the secret tunnel that lets your brain hear a richer version of yourself.
required_facts: Brain uses two pathways to hear speech

story_arc.purpose: Context – explain why the question matters
story_arc.reveal: Knowing this changes how we design microphones, hearing aids, and even therapy for voice disorders.
required_facts: Perception of self‑voice is crucial for communication

story_arc.reveal: When you speak, sound waves leave your mouth and travel through the air to your outer ear.
required_facts: Air‑conduction is the usual way external sounds reach the ear

story_arc.reveal: Simultaneously, vibrations from your vocal folds and skull travel through bone directly to the cochlea.
required_facts: Bone‑conduction adds a low‑frequency boost and tactile cue

story_arc.reveal: The skull acts as a low‑pass filter, amplifying deep tones that you feel in your jaw and skin.
required_facts: Low‑pass effect makes self‑voice sound richer and deeper

story_arc.reveal: Your brain merges the airy sound and the bone‑conduction signal into a single, familiar self‑voice representation.
required_facts: Somatosensory feedback is part of the perception

story_arc.purpose: Fourth Reveal – what a mic misses
story_arc.reveal: A microphone records only the airborne component, stripping away the bone‑conduction boost and tactile feel.
When you play back the recording, the brain detects a mismatch: no deep tones, no vibrations, so the voice feels higher and stranger.
required_facts: Absence of low frequencies and tactile cues causes the “foreign” feeling

story_arc.purpose: Final Reveal – why it never changes
story_arc.reveal: Even after repeated listening, the physical difference stays; you just get used to the new version, not the original.
required_facts: Familiarity reduces surprise but not the acoustic gap

ending_payoff: So the next time you hear your own voice on a recording, remember: the microphone left out the hidden tunnel that makes your voice feel like home. That’s why it sounds so different—and why your brain knows the difference right away.
